passages.title: From Twigs to Tech: The Evolution of the Toothbrush

paragraphs.text: Although your own toothbrush should not be more than three or four months old, according to the World Health Organization and the American Dental Association, toothbrushes have a history spanning thousands of years. People of today are aware that their mornings and evenings should include flossing, mouthwash, and two minutes of teeth-brushing. Last year in the United States, people spent $189 billion in the pursuit of healthy teeth. But even long before now, ancient civilizations understood that if they did not clean their teeth, they would fall out. In fact, the earliest known "toothbrush" was not a brush at all—it was a chew stick.

Today, our electric toothbrushes do most, if not all, of the work for the toothbrusher. However, chew sticks used in ancient Babylon and Egypt required significantly more effort. First, the right twig or plant stem would be harvested and, if necessary, soaked overnight. Next, one end was broken down to separate the stick's fibers so it could reach around and between the teeth. The other end was sharpened to a narrow point. Finally, the frayed end would be used to brush buildup off the teeth. The narrow point was used to pick between the teeth. This method prevailed for thousands of years, until being replaced by the Miswak.

Around 600 C.E., over 4,000 years after the known advent of chew-stick usage, the use of Miswak started spreading. Originating in the Islamic world, this type of chew stick is made from the Salvadora persica tree. It contains natural minerals such as fluoride and silica that actually help strengthen teeth and kill bacteria. Today, many people in parts of the Middle East and Africa still use the Miswak because of its natural effectiveness.

It was during the Tang Dynasty (619–907 C.E.) in China that the first bristle-style, handled toothbrush was invented. The Chinese used coarse hairs from the back of a Siberian wild hog's neck. These hairs were stiff and sturdy, making them perfect for scrubbing away disease-causing plaque and tartar. The bristles were attached to handles made of bamboo or animal bone. When travelers from Europe visited China, they brought these "bristle brushes" back with them. However, the idea did not catch on immediately in the West. Europeans thought the hog hair was too stiff and preferred softer feathers or sponges. Unfortunately, those were not as effective at cleaning between and around teeth.

For centuries, Europeans continued using linens and pastes to polish their teeth. But as the amount of carbohydrates in people's diet steadily increased, the effectiveness of linens and paste decreased. Carbohydrates convert to sugars, and the bacteria in people's mouths feed on the sugars, producing acids that eat away at the teeth's protective enamel. The materials that most of the Western world relied on for dental health were becoming outdated because they were no longer effective. There were some effective toothbrushes available, but they were handcrafted and too expensive for most people. Fortunately, an affordable new product would be heading to the market in the late 1700s.

In 1780, Englishman William Addis started the first Western company to mass-produce toothbrushes. Legend says Addis was sitting in a prison cell for starting a riot. He was comparing the rags and soot used to clean teeth with the brooms sweeping the floors. He decided there had to be a better way to brush teeth. He used a small animal bone from his meal, bored tiny holes into it, and tied tufts of animal hair through with wire. Thus was born the prototype of the first toothbrush that would be mass-produced.

Unfortunately, mass-produced does not mean mass-improved. The animal-hair bristles stayed wet for a long time and harbored bacteria. Everything changed in 1938 when the chemical company DuPont invented nylon. Nylon was perfect for mass-produced toothbrushes because it was cheap, its stiffness could be controlled, and it dried quickly. The modern toothbrush had arrived, but modern hygiene practices in the West had further to go.

In the early 1900s, only 7% of American households were brushing their teeth. The practice was often dismissed as a luxury or unnecessary. It was not until after World War II that oral hygiene became a major priority. U.S. soldiers were required to brush their teeth twice a day to prevent dental infections. When the soldiers returned home, they brought this habit with them. This sparked a nationwide trend in the United States that continues to this day.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Global
Getting to the Answer: Since the stem contains the phrase "overall structure," this is a Global question, and the Main Idea in your Roadmap will be a helpful tool. The passage is about the history of the toothbrush and the long time it took to arrive in the West. Paragraph 8 is about how toothbrushing became more common in the U.S. after World War II. Use this to form a prediction. (B) correctly identifies that the paragraph gives the history of toothbrushing in the U.S. since the early 1900s: few people brushed, soldiers brushed during WWII, soldiers brought the practice home, and the practice spread. (A) is incorrect because, while it is accurate, it does not connect to the "overall structure" of the passage, which emphasizes the toothbrush's history. Furthermore, "cultural practices in the United States" is far too broad to refer to tooth care only. (C) is Opposite. The passage states that people "dismissed" teethbrushing. (D) is incorrect because it is Out of Scope. The paragraph does not summarize the entire history of the toothbrush, only toothbrushing in the U.S. since 1900.

options.A: The first documented chew sticks, made from the Salvadora persica tree, originated in Babylon and Egypt; the Miswak, from the Islamic world, is still used in the Middle East and Africa; during the Tang Dynasty in China, bristle-and-handled toothbrushes were made; and, finally, hand-crafted toothbrushes were all that was used in Europe before the 1700s.

solution.exhibit_text:
Category: Inference
Getting to the Answer: For questions summarizing parts of a passage, reference your Roadmap to help you briskly eliminate the incorrect choices. Eliminate (B) because the first chew sticks were found in Babylon and Egypt, while the Miswak originated in the Islamic world. (C) correctly summarizes the passage. On test day, select that choice with confidence and move on. But for reference, note that (D) is incorrect because it places the developments out of order, incorrectly placing the Tang Dynasty toothbrush as earliest.

passages.title: The Ball that Defied Logic

paragraphs.text: In the 1870s, a baseball pitcher named William "Candy" Cummings threw a ball that astounded crowds across the eastern United States. Instead of flying through the air in a straight line, as one might expect it to do, Cummings's ball seemed to change its path midway to the batter. To the naked eye, this pitch appeared to curve, not only impressing spectators but also completely fooling batters of the day who attempted to make contact. This "curveball" changed the way baseball was played and continues to be an essential tool for the professional game.

Interest in this phenomenon excited the world of sports and compelled scientists to investigate the mechanism by which a thrown baseball could change its path mid-flight. Some posited that the rotation of Earth played a factor. Others theorized that the effect was simply the work of a foreign object upon the ball. In reality, the curve of a curveball involves a complex scientific process called the Magnus effect, named after German physicist H. G. Magnus. While this effect was eventually identified in the late nineteenth century as the reason for the curveball, the origins of the explanation actually date back as far as the time of Isaac Newton. The physics of an object moving inside a fluid substance such as a liquid or a gas—in this case, a baseball flying through the air—can be complex and unexpected. When a ball leaves the pitcher's hand with a bit of a spin, its turning motion drags some of the surrounding air with it. While the ball spins in the air, the speed of the air changes, and the air moves more slowly on one side of the ball than it does on the other side. This difference in speed causes the ball to depart from its straight path, making the ball curve. A skilled pitcher can learn to create this effect by imparting a spin upon the ball as it is released.

This unexpected movement of the ball can have devastating results for the batter. Because of the Magnus effect, a curveball will begin its directional change, or "break," in the opposite direction of the pitcher's throwing hand (for example, toward the right side if the pitcher is left-handed). A ball that spins in this manner is now referred to as a "regulation curve." In the early 1900s, pitchers began throwing curveballs in the opposite direction as well; these have come to be known as "fadeaways" or "screwballs." In both types of curves, the effect is generally the same. The ball has already changed its direction, and the batter has swung at a ball that was never really there. Today, the curveball is still alive and well, living in the nightmares of batters who have attempted—and failed—to hit it.
